paragraphs.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 (LDS5) is a connective tissue disorder caused by heterozygous mutation in the TGFB3 gene. Its systemic features overlap with those of Loeys-Dietz, Shprintzen-Goldberg, and Marfan syndromes. They include cleft palate or bifid uvula, hypertelorism, skeletal overgrowth or growth retardation, arachnodactyly, joint hyperextensibility, cervical spine instability, and clubfoot (Rienhoff et al., 2013; Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015; Kuechler et al., 2015). Cardiovascular involvement is highly variable. It includes thoracic and abdominal aortic aneurysm and dissection and mitral valve disease (Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) described a 9-year-old European American girl born to nonconsanguineous parents. At birth she had contractures of the right hand, most severe in the third and fourth fingers, as well as contractures of all toes, together with a midline facial nevus flammeus and mild hypotonia. Her birth weight was 2.9 kg (5th centile). At 3 months she was evaluated for failure to thrive and delayed gross motor function. At 17 months she weighed 7.5 kg (less than the 1st centile). Findings at that age included pes planus, mild pectus excavatum, hyperextensibility of multiple large joints, mild retrognathia, prominent eyes, hypertelorism, bifid uvula with an intact hard palate, a small metopic ridge, blue sclerae, decreased bulk of all appendicular and axial muscles, low tone, diminished reflexes, and markedly reduced subcutaneous fat. She stood independently with a positive Gowers sign at 20 months and walked with a 'hip waddle' at 24 months. Her neurocognitive development was appropriate for age. Radiographs showed bilateral coxa valga. A quadriceps muscle biopsy at age 7 years showed type 1 fiber predominance with mild, focal type 1 fiber disproportion, consistent with disuse, and no dystrophic or inflammatory changes. Yearly echocardiograms from 18 months showed no cardiac defect, and her aortic root dimension at age 6.5 years was normal (z score 0.39). The authors noted that she did not meet diagnostic criteria for Marfan, Beals-Hecht, or Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with autosomal dominant features overlapping Marfan syndrome and LDS. Seven family members aged 40 to 68 years had aneurysms and dissections, mainly of the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta. Three of them died of aortic dissection and rupture. Four family members had mitral valve abnormalities ranging from mild prolapse to severe regurgitation. Craniofacial features were subtle and included a long face, high-arched palate, and retrognathia. Pectus deformity and scoliosis were frequent. Other recurrent findings were velvety skin, varices, and hiatal hernia. Autoimmune features included HLA-B27-positive spondyloarthritis, Graves disease, and celiac disease. Pathology reports from 2 deceased patients described extensive elastic fiber fragmentation and aortic medial degeneration.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) summarized 43 patients from 11 families with TGFB3 mutations. Vascular involvement ranged from no cardiovascular abnormalities at age 64 to type A aortic dissection (median age 51 years, range 40 to 80) or type B aortic dissection (median age 44.5 years, range 30 to 57), abdominal aortic dissection, and death from cerebral aneurysm dissection at age 55. No early arterial dissection, dissection at small aortic dimension, or striking arterial tortuosity was observed. Other cardiovascular findings included mitral valve disease, persistent foramen ovale, and atrial or ventricular septal defects. Common LDS features were hypertelorism (14 patients), bifid uvula (11), cleft palate (5), cervical spine instability, and clubfoot. Other recurrent features were dolichocephaly, high-arched palate, retrognathia, tall stature (12), joint hypermobility (9), arachnodactyly (16), pectus deformity (8), kyphoscoliosis (11), and inguinal hernia. Early-onset osteoarthritis was reported in 2 individuals. One patient with the D263H mutation had short stature. The authors noted striking intrafamilial and interfamilial clinical variability.
